findings.title: strategy.close() destroys the factory-shared queue pool, breaking rebalances
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but the `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and shared across every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo closes/recreates the strategy on every partition rebalance, so after the first revoke the pool's worker threads are dead and its queues are shut down, while `factory.queue_pool` is still non-None. The next `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker()` will happily build a strategy over the dead pool and every submitted message will be silently dropped (or raise on `put` into a shut-down queue), stalling the consumer until the process is restarted.

findings.title: commit function invoked from a background thread
findings.body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which ends up in arroyo's `Commit` callback and ultimately the Kafka consumer. Arroyo strategies are documented as being driven from the single processing thread; the underlying consumer and the processor's offset bookkeeping are not thread-safe. Concurrent `commit()` from this thread while the main loop polls/commits can corrupt offset state or raise from librdkafka, risking duplicate or lost processing.

findings.title: OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation
findings.body: `OffsetTracker` lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, and there is no API to drop state for revoked partitions. After a rebalance, `last_committed`, `all_offsets` and `outstanding` still contain entries for partitions this consumer no longer owns, so the commit thread can emit commits for partitions owned by another member, and stale `last_committed` values for a re-assigned partition can suppress legitimate commits (the loop only commits offsets greater than `last_committed`, which may now be far ahead of the new fetch position).

findings.title: queue.ShutDown / Queue.shutdown require Python 3.13
findings.body: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown(immediate=...)` were added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, `except queue.ShutDown` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` raises `AttributeError` when an exception propagates, and `q.shutdown(...)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` raises `AttributeError` which is swallowed by the bare `except Exception`. The result is that workers block forever in `work_queue.get()` (the `self.shutdown` flag is only checked between items), so shutdown takes 5s per worker and in-flight work is abandoned. If 3.13 is a hard requirement it should be stated; otherwise use a sentinel item plus `get(timeout=...)`.

findings.title: Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim
findings.body: The docstrings for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` and `FixedQueuePool` claim "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow `result_processor` therefore causes unbounded growth of queued `WorkItem`s (each holding the full Kafka `Message`), leading to OOM rather than backpressure, and the comment is misleading. Give the queues a maxsize and raise `MessageRejected` when full.

findings.title: Lock creation relies on CPython dict atomicity
findings.body: `_get_partition_lock` does an unsynchronized `get` followed by `setdefault` on a plain dict. This happens to be safe only because of CPython's GIL making `setdefault` atomic; it is not guaranteed by the language and would break under a free-threaded build. Prefer a single module-level lock guarding lock creation, or a `defaultdict(threading.Lock)` created once under a lock.

findings.title: Transaction name hardcodes 'monitors' prefix for remote subscriptions worker
findings.body: The sentry transaction name is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this is generic remote-subscription/uptime code. Including `worker_id` also produces high-cardinality transaction names (one per queue). This will make the uptime consumer's traces show up under misleading `monitors.*` names.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts nothing meaningful about offsets
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` ends with `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which is a tautology (both branches assert the same thing) and, more importantly, contradicts the test's stated intent that "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" — the implementation does commit offsets after a failure (the worker completes the offset in `finally`). The assertion will pass even if commits are completely broken; it should assert the expected committed offset (102).

findings.title: Kafka integration test drives StreamProcessor via private APIs and sleeps
findings.body: `test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` calls `processor._run_once()` / `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo APIs that can change without notice) and busy-loops for a fixed 5 seconds, which makes the test both brittle against arroyo upgrades and slow/flaky under load. The `commits_made` assertions are also guarded by `if commits_made:` so they silently no-op if no commit was recorded.
